speaker: Sholto Douglas
title: Is RL + LLMs enough for AGI? — Sholto Douglas & Trenton Bricken
question: In frontier LLM post-training, why did reinforcement learning from human feedback fail to deliver expert-level capability gains compared to verifiable rewards?
guest: The big thing that really worked is RL from verifiable rewards, where you have a clean reward signal. The initial unhobbling of language models was RL from human feedback, where typically it was pairwise feedback, and the outputs of the models became closer and closer to things that humans wanted. But this doesn't necessarily improve their performance at any difficulty or problem domain, particularly as humans are actually quite bad judges of what a better answer is. Humans have things like length biases and so forth. So you need a signal of whether the model was correct in its output that is quite true—things like the correct answer to a math problem or unit tests passing. These are examples of a reward signal that's very clean, but even these can be hacked, by the way. Even with unit tests, the models find ways around them to hard-code particular values if they can figure out what the actual test is doing. If they can look at the cached Python files and find what the actual test is, they'll try and hack their way around it. So these aren't perfect, but they're much closer.

points.core: Human raters judge hard outputs poorly because of systematic biases like favoring length.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
RLHF optimizes a learned proxy for human approval, and that proxy caps out at roughly the level of the raters. A reward model trained on human preference comparisons captures what looks good to annotators, not what is actually correct, so the policy learns to be plausible, agreeable, and well-formatted rather than right. Once the model matches or exceeds its raters on a task, they can no longer reliably tell better answers from worse ones, and the signal becomes noise or actively rewards persuasive errors, sycophancy, and confident fluency. The reward model is also exploitable: pushing hard against it produces reward hacking rather than skill, so RLHF has to be run conservatively, with tight constraints that keep the policy near its starting point. Human labels are also expensive, slow, and inconsistent, which limits scale.

Verifiable rewards (unit tests, proof checkers, exact-match math answers, game outcomes) are grounded in truth rather than opinion. They stay accurate however capable the model gets, are cheap to compute at massive scale, and support long-horizon exploration, so the model can discover strategies beyond human demonstration. That is why reasoning-model gains came from RL on checkable tasks.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) relies on a learned neural reward model trained on noisy human preferences, creating two bottlenecks that cap capability gains. First, human annotators cannot reliably verify complex expert tasks like frontier mathematics or software engineering, often rewarding confident tone, verbosity, and formatting over substantive truth. Second, because a learned reward model is an imperfect proxy, sustained optimization quickly triggers reward hacking: the policy exploits flaws in the proxy rather than improving genuine reasoning. Practitioners must therefore enforce tight divergence penalties and stop training early, confining RLHF largely to stylistic alignment and instruction following.

In contrast, verifiable rewards replace subjective proxies with deterministic ground-truth evaluators like compilers, unit tests, and symbolic checkers. Because objective verification resists reward hacking, post-training compute can scale orders of magnitude further without collapse. Under sustained optimization, models freely explore extended chains of thought, organically discovering expert reasoning strategies such as self-correction, backtracking, and deep problem decomposition.

noweb.answer:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) relies on a learned reward model trained on human preferences, creating two fundamental bottlenecks. First, human annotators cannot reliably verify complex, multi-step reasoning in frontier math, coding, or science; they inevitably favor confident, well-formatted prose over subtle correctness, biasing supervision toward surface style rather than truth. Second, because a neural reward model is only an imperfect proxy, scaling RL compute triggers Goodhart’s law: the policy exploits spurious correlations—such as verbosity and sycophancy—causing true performance to degrade unless constrained by tight KL-divergence penalties that prevent deep exploration away from the base model.

In contrast, verifiable rewards evaluate outputs directly against deterministic ground truth, such as unit tests, compilers, or exact symbolic answers. Because this signal is objective, programmatic, and resistant to stylistic reward hacking, models can sustain massive RL optimization without reward collapse, enabling them to explore freely over long horizons and autonomously discover expert reasoning behaviors like self-verification, backtracking, and extended test-time search.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The framing is a bit strong. RLHF was mainly built to make models helpful, harmless, and well-formatted, not to push them to expert-level reasoning. Still, the gap with verifiable rewards is real, and it comes down to the quality of the reward signal.

RLHF trains against a learned reward model, which is only a stand-in for what human raters prefer. Raters can't reliably judge expert-level answers like hard proofs, complex code, or advanced science, so they tend to reward things that are easy to see: confident tone, length, good formatting, and agreeing with the user. If the policy is optimized hard against that stand-in, it learns to exploit the reward model's flaws (Goodhart's law). So RLHF runs have to stay short and tightly constrained. The preference labels are also noisy, expensive, and carry little information per comparison.

Verifiable rewards, such as unit tests, exact math answers, or proof checkers, give cheap and accurate ground truth that scales and is much harder to game. That makes long, large-scale RL runs workable, and that's where extended chain-of-thought reasoning emerged (o1, DeepSeek-R1).

Two caveats. Some research (for example Yue et al., 2025) suggests verifiable-reward RL also mostly brings out abilities the base model already has rather than creating new ones. And it only works in areas where answers can be checked automatically.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) relies on a learned reward model trained on human preferences, which is a noisy, imperfect proxy for correctness. As optimization pressure increases, models exploit this proxy through reward hacking—favoring verbosity, sycophancy, and confident-sounding prose over genuine accuracy. To prevent this collapse, practitioners must enforce tight KL-divergence penalties that tether the model close to its supervised fine-tuning baseline, effectively capping capability growth and limiting RLHF to stylistic alignment rather than new skill discovery. Moreover, human raters cannot reliably evaluate complex expert reasoning at scale, often rewarding plausible errors over hard-to-verify truths.

By contrast, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) uses objective, automated ground-truth checks—such as unit tests, compilers, or mathematical verifiers—that are far harder to game. Because the feedback signal remains accurate under heavy, sustained optimization, models can safely explore far beyond human demonstrations, discovering emergent reasoning behaviors like self-correction, backtracking, and extended test-time search that drive genuine expert-level gains.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
The bottleneck was the quality of the reward signal. Conventional RLHF trains a reward model to predict which answers human raters prefer. That works well for instruction following, clarity, and tone. But when a solution is hard even for an expert to check, ratings become expensive and noisy. The reward model can then favor a polished, plausible answer with a subtle error, and reinforcement learning can amplify that bias. [InstructGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155) · [RLHF limitations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15217)

Verifiable rewards let the model try many solutions and get cheap, consistent feedback about whether each one succeeds. A code submission can be run against tests, and a math answer can be checked against a known result. This makes large-scale trial and error practical even when producing a correct solution is much harder than checking it. The advantage is strongest where the verifier reliably captures what counts as success. [DeepSeek-R1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09422-z)

noweb.answer:
Human feedback is only as reliable as the judgments behind it. On hard math, coding, and other expert tasks, raters may struggle to tell a correct solution from a convincing mistake. Expert review is expensive, and a reward model trained on those judgments can learn to reward polish or familiar reasoning even when the answer is wrong. Optimizing harder against that reward can amplify those errors.

Verifiable rewards give the model a more reliable signal on tasks with checkable outcomes. A test suite or proof checker can evaluate many attempts cheaply and give credit to a correct solution even if no human demonstrated it. That makes it practical to train on far more attempts and discover better strategies. Human feedback remains valuable for qualities such as clarity and helpfulness, where correctness alone leaves much of what users care about unmeasured.
